There is the consensus going around, that this is supposed to be a soft launch mainly targeting the Nintendo Fanbase. Next holiday season, where Nintendo has Mario, Zelda and a whole lot of other games ready is when the mass market appeal should really begin.

They are definitely attempting a maximum attach rate strategy. In March you will buy Zelda. Then in April you will buy Mario Kart. Then you will buy Splatoon 2. Because these are the only major AAA games worth buying month after month. There are some good indie games to help fill the gaps, but they won't sell the system, or keep you picking it up in the absence of good AAA software.

I'm not sure how this strategy will work. But it's probably the best Nintendo can manage with their frequent software draughts and lack of third party support. Better to release a AAA first party game every month or two than dump them all at once and have a year of little new software. That's how the Switch would end up collecting just as much dust as the Wii U.

They need to get onboard with 3rd parties. Dangle some carrots like:

1) Reduce royalty rate for AAA game delivered during the first 6 months

2) Make the developer tools plentiful, documented and easy to use. Much as people rip on MS, this is where they shine and it counts.

3) Send Nintendo devs on loan to 3rd party to actively code, consult and nurture.

4) Strike a deal with a 3rd party pack in game with the system.

I hear they've gotten much better on 2, but the rest would certainly go a long ways towards helping.

I think the biggest thing that helps is they finally have hardware of a similar profile to the competition. Maybe not in raw power, but at least it's back on the same page in terms of basic input and output. No more dual screens, no more sacrificing buttons for waggle, no more forced motion controls, no more forced touch input.
